description: Types of school in England: comprehensive, grammar, academy, free, private and faith schools.
content_html:
Why Does School Type Matter?

The UK has a diverse education system. Different types of school reflect different political priorities — about selection, competition, the role of the market, and who education is for. Sociologists from different perspectives disagree about whether this diversity is a strength or a source of inequality. Understanding the structural variety of school types is a distinct requirement in GCSE Sociology because the type of school a pupil attends shapes the opportunities available to them.

Key Fact

The main types of school in the UK are: comprehensive schools, grammar schools, academies, free schools, private (independent) schools and faith schools.

Primary and Secondary Education

State education in England and Wales is divided into primary schools (ages 5–11) and secondary schools (ages 11–16 or 18). The vast majority of children attend state schools funded by central government. Compulsory state education was introduced in the nineteenth century and gradually extended; all children in England must be in some form of education or training until the age of 18.

Comprehensive, Grammar and Selective Schools

Following the Education Act 1944, England adopted the tripartite system of grammar, technical and secondary modern schools, with pupils allocated by the eleven-plus examination. From the 1960s onwards, most local authorities replaced this with comprehensive schools that accept pupils of all abilities. Comprehensive education was associated with the principle that selection by ability at age eleven disadvantaged working-class children.

Grammar schools survive in parts of England. Supporters argue they provide high-achieving pupils from all backgrounds with access to a rigorous academic education. Critics — including many sociologists — argue that grammar schools entrench class inequality because middle-class families can afford private tuition to prepare their children for the eleven-plus while working-class families typically cannot. Welsh secondary schools are almost entirely comprehensive, with grammar schools remaining largely an English phenomenon.

Academies and Free Schools

Academies are state-funded but operate outside local authority control, with greater freedom over curriculum, pay and admissions. Free schools were introduced as a related policy and can be set up by any group — parents, teachers, charities or faith organisations — required to be non-selective and non-fee-paying. The expansion of academies and free schools is linked to the marketisation of education. The market logic assumes that competition between schools for pupils drives up standards. Sociologist Stephen Ball argued that marketisation benefits middle-class families who have the cultural capital and social networks to navigate school choice, while working-class families are disadvantaged.

Private and Faith Schools

Private schools — also called independent or public schools — are funded by fees and private endowments rather than the state. Approximately 7% of pupils in England attend private schools. Sociologists note that this small minority produces a disproportionate share of senior politicians, judges, top civil servants and university entrants to highly selective institutions, raising questions about whether private schooling reinforces class inequality and limits social mobility.

Faith schools are state-funded schools with a religious character, provided by faith organisations in partnership with the government. They exist across England and Wales and include Church of England, Roman Catholic, Jewish, Muslim and other faith communities. Faith schools may select a proportion of their intake on the basis of religious practice. From a functionalist perspective, faith schools transmit shared cultural values within communities. Critics — particularly from feminist and secular perspectives — argue that some faith schools reinforce gender inequality through their curriculum and expectations, or disadvantage pupils from different religious backgrounds in selective admissions.

Functionalist: A diverse range of school types allows the education system to match individuals to the roles best suited to their abilities, supporting meritocratic role allocation. Grammar schools and academies are seen as providing academic pathways for talented pupils from any background.

Marxist: The existence of fee-paying private schools alongside state schools reflects and reinforces class inequality. The bourgeoisie purchases educational advantage for their children, ensuring that privileged social positions are passed on rather than earned on merit.

Feminist: Historically, many elite schools were single-sex institutions designed for boys. Feminists have highlighted how comprehensive co-education improved girls’ access to the full curriculum, but argue that gender inequalities persist through subject choices and teacher expectations even within mixed schools. Some faith schools may reinforce traditional gender roles through their ethos.

New Right: Supporters of marketisation argue that parental choice and school competition drive up standards for all. Free schools and academies are welcomed as breaking the monopoly of local authority control and giving parents greater agency in choosing their children’s education.

Ball’s research on school choice showed that middle-class parents use their cultural capital to navigate the competitive market: they read league tables, visit multiple schools, write effective appeals and move into desirable catchment areas to access high-performing schools. Working-class parents make equally genuine choices but lack the same information, social networks and mobility. Ball’s argument is that the language of “parental choice” disguises a process that systematically advantages already privileged families, concentrating advantage and reinforcing the class gap in educational outcomes.

Key Fact

Both academies and free schools are state-funded but operate outside local authority control. The key difference is origin: academies are typically converted from existing state schools, while free schools are newly created by parents, charities or other groups. Both reflect the marketisation of education — the application of market principles (competition, consumer choice, performance measurement) to schooling.
exam_tip_html:
On a 12-mark Evaluate question about school types or marketisation, avoid treating the question as a factual recall task. Present the New Right and functionalist case for school diversity and competition, then challenge it using Marxist evidence on private school advantage and Ball’s research on how middle-class families benefit most from parental choice. A strong answer names at least two perspectives with named sociologists and reaches a supported conclusion about whether school diversity increases or entrenches inequality.

On a 2-mark Define question, give a definition rather than an example. If asked to define ‘marketisation of education’, do not just say “schools competing” — explain what it means: the application of market principles (competition, parental choice, performance measures) to the organisation of schooling.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK has a diverse system of school types — state, private, comprehensive, grammar, academy, free school and faith school — each reflecting different values about selection, competition and equality of opportunity.
  • Marketisation (academies, free schools, parental choice) is welcomed by the New Right and functionalists as driving up standards, but Marxists and Ball argue it primarily advantages middle-class families with the cultural capital to navigate school choice.
  • Private schools charge fees that give the wealthy a significant educational advantage: approximately 7% of pupils attend them, yet they produce a disproportionate share of elite professionals, raising persistent questions about class inequality and social mobility.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a free school?
A) A state school that charges no fees because state education is free
B) A state-funded school set up by parents, charities or other groups outside local authority control
C) A school that selects pupils on academic ability via the eleven-plus
D) A school funded by a religious organisation with selective admissions
practice_questions.marks: B) A state-funded school set up by parents, charities or other groups outside local authority control [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying the application of market principles to education; 1 mark for explaining what this means in practice. Example: 'Marketisation of education is the process by which market principles — competition between schools for pupils, parental choice and performance measures such as league tables — are applied to the organisation of schooling, on the assumption that competition drives up standards.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one sociological argument against grammar schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid argument (e.g. grammar schools entrench class inequality / middle-class families can afford eleven-plus tutoring / working-class pupils are disproportionately excluded); 2 marks for a developed description naming the mechanism. Example: 'Critics of grammar schools argue that they entrench class inequality because middle-class families have the resources to pay for private tuition to prepare their children for the eleven-plus examination, while working-class families typically cannot. The result is that grammar schools disproportionately serve middle-class pupils rather than the academically talented from all backgrounds that their supporters claim they serve.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Ball's argument about how marketisation of education reinforces social class inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Ball argued that middle-class parents use their cultural capital to navigate the competitive school market: they read and interpret league tables, visit multiple schools, write effective appeals and use social networks to access information. Working-class parents care equally but lack the same information and resources, making 'parental choice' less meaningful in practice. Point 2: Middle-class families can also move into the catchment areas of high-performing schools — a strategy requiring both economic resources and the cultural knowledge of which schools are worth pursuing. Ball's conclusion is that market competition reinforces existing class inequalities rather than levelling the playing field, concentrating advantage among families already most privileged.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that having different types of school benefits all pupils in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments for: functionalists argue school diversity allows meritocratic role allocation (grammar schools channel academic pupils, vocational routes others); New Right argues competition drives up standards for all schools. Arguments against: Marxists argue private schools allow the bourgeoisie to purchase educational advantage, passing privilege across generations rather than allocating it on merit; Ball's research shows marketisation advantages middle-class families; grammar schools disproportionately serve middle-class pupils who can afford eleven-plus tutoring. Feminist perspective: historically school types were designed around male education; comprehensive co-education improved gender equality, but some faith schools may reinforce gendered expectations. At least two perspectives with named sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement. Secure (5-7): Both sides, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (3-4): Mostly one-sided, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that private schools are the main cause of educational inequality in contemporary Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments for: private schools concentrate educational advantage for the wealthy; approximately 7% of pupils but a disproportionate share of elite professionals; Marxist argument that the bourgeoisie purchases intergenerational privilege through fee-paying schools. Arguments against or complicating: class inequality also operates within the state sector (Ball on marketisation, Halsey on class barriers even with comprehensive schooling); grammar schools within the state sector also create selection-based inequality accessible to those who can afford tutoring; other factors such as material deprivation and cultural capital produce inequality regardless of private schooling. A judgement that weighs whether private schools are the main cause or one factor among several. Comparison of perspectives explicit. Secure (7-9): Most arguments present, named sociologists, clear judgement. Developing (4-6): One-sided or undeveloped, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the tripartite system introduced by the 1944 Education Act?
options: A system of grammar, technical and secondary modern schools with selection by eleven-plus
A system dividing education into primary, secondary and further stages
Three funding streams: state, academy and private
A system of three core subjects taught in all schools

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologist argued that marketisation of education primarily benefits middle-class families who can navigate parental choice?
Both academies and free schools are state-funded but operate outside ______ authority control, reflecting the marketisation of education.
Approximately ______% of pupils in England attend private (fee-paying) schools, yet they produce a disproportionate share of elite professionals.
Match each school type to its key characteristic.
right: Admits pupils of all abilities; no academic selection
Selects pupils on academic ability via the eleven-plus examination
State-funded but independent of local authority control, often with a sponsor
Set up by parents, charities or other groups; state-funded and non-selective

flashcard_questions.a: A state secondary school that admits pupils of all abilities without academic selection.
A state secondary school that selects pupils by academic ability, usually via the eleven-plus examination.
A selection examination taken at age eleven to determine which type of secondary school a pupil attends.
A state-funded school operating independently of local authority control, often with greater freedom over curriculum and admissions.
A state-funded school set up by parents, charities or other groups outside local authority control, required to be non-selective.
A state-funded school with a religious character provided by a faith organisation in partnership with the government.
The application of market principles to schooling, so that schools compete for pupils and are judged on performance measures.
The post-1944 secondary education system dividing pupils into grammar, technical and secondary modern schools by eleven-plus.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sociologist linked marketisation to middle-class advantage in school choice?
Why do Marxists criticise private schools?
flashcard_questions.a: They allow the bourgeoisie to purchase educational advantage for their children, passing privilege across generations rather than allocating it on merit.

glossary_terms.definition: A state secondary school that admits pupils of all abilities without selection by academic test.
A state secondary school that selects pupils on academic ability, usually through the eleven-plus examination.
The application of market principles including competition, parental choice and performance measures such as league tables to the organisation of schooling.
A state-funded school that operates independently of local authority control, with greater freedoms over curriculum, pay and admissions.
A state-funded school set up by parents, charities, businesses or other groups, operating outside local authority control and required to be non-selective.
A state-funded school with a religious character, provided by a faith organisation in partnership with the government, which may give priority in admissions to pupils of that faith.
The post-war secondary education system in England divided into grammar, technical and secondary modern schools, with pupils allocated by the eleven-plus examination.
